concept.name: Correlation breakdown
concept.definition: The empirically documented tendency for correlations between markets and assets to rise sharply in bear markets and crises - but not in bull markets - so that diversification benefits shrink precisely when they are most needed; Longin and Solnik (2001) established the asymmetry formally using extreme value theory.
concept.intuition: In a panic, everything sells off together: the low correlations that justified your diversification in calm times evaporate in the crash.
concept.mechanics: Longin and Solnik model the tails of the multivariate return distribution with extreme value theory and test exceedance correlations; they find conditional correlation between international equity markets increases strongly in bear markets but not in bull markets, rejecting multivariate normality in the negative tail only. They also warn that naive tests conditioning on absolute return size spuriously link correlation to volatility.
concept.failure_modes: As a finding it indicts static models: any risk estimate assuming constant correlation (including constant-correlation GARCH) understates joint crash risk. Conversely, simplistic studies that condition on large absolute returns confuse conditioning effects with true correlation shifts.
concept.misconceptions: It is not literally true that 'all correlations go to one': the documented effect is an asymmetric increase in bear markets related to market trend rather than to volatility per se, and positive extreme returns show no corresponding increase.
concept.example: In the 2008 crisis, developed-market equity indexes that normally correlated around 0.5 fell together far more tightly; Longin-Solnik's earlier US-UK analysis already showed exceedance correlation of 0.578 on the downside versus 0.226 on the upside.

citations.source: Longin and Solnik, Extreme Correlation of International Equity Markets, Journal of Finance 56(2), 649-676
